messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Somchai was a 66-year-old roofer from a South Eastern Asian family who had built his life around physical work, early mornings, and the pride of being the one who could still carry shingles up a ladder before younger men were fully awake. The event that changed that steadiness came years after he had already spent a long day on a roof. A hidden pocket of toxic chemical exposure, encountered while repairing a damaged section of an older building, left him suddenly overwhelmed and frightened in a way he had never experienced. What he remembers most is not a single dramatic image but the details that lodged in him: the sharp hospital smell when he was taken for treatment, the dark of the ambulance and later the way nighttime in the ward seemed to close in around him, and the sickening, related chemical smell that seemed to cling to his clothes and skin. Since then, those same smells and any waking moment in the dark have become potent reminders; when they appear, Somchai immediately pulls back from the feeling, tries hard not to think about what happened, and clamps down on his reactions, because he fears that if he lets himself stay with it he will lose control.

Yet the more he tries to shut it out, the more the event returns. He describes the memories as a film that plays over and over, vividly detailed, with the same sequence of events arriving uninvited and, at times, without any clear picture at all—just the full emotional intensity flooding him back as if his body remembers before his mind does. Those recollections have fed the sense that he cannot rely on himself, that he failed to protect his own body once and may do so again. He has come to believe that his future is already damaged, that there is no real future left to plan for, and that the world is a dangerous place that can turn hazardous without warning. Those beliefs have shaped the way he lives. He avoids unfamiliar places because he cannot assess the danger there, and he has become careful in the extreme never to disagree or assert himself, even with clients or family, because conflict now feels like another situation he might not be able to handle. He also dwells on how he used to be before the event—stronger, calmer, less guarded—and that comparison leaves him more convinced that the man he was is gone for good.

In daily life, these patterns keep the alarm going. When a faint hospital-like odor drifts through a clinic waiting room, or when a smell related to the chemicals on the job appears in a garage, basement, or on a worksite, Somchai feels his body tighten and his mind drift back to the roof and the ambulance, and he then redoubles his efforts to avoid thinking about it. The attempt to suppress the memories often leaves him more keyed up, unable to relax even when he knows he is in a safe place, and his concentration slips at work and at home. On the job he has begun staying close to familiar houses and routes, turning down unfamiliar assignments, and letting others make the decisions so he does not have to face anything uncertain; at home, he becomes more withdrawn and guarded, which has quietly changed how he and his wife talk to one another. The more he avoids, the more the world seems dangerous, and the more dangerous it seems, the more he braces himself against it. That bracing keeps his attention fixed on possible threats, and the constant scanning only seems to pull up more fragments of the event, as if the mind cannot stop rehearsing what happened.

By the time he sought help, Somchai was exhausted by how little relief he could find, especially at night. Waking in the dark now brings the whole chain back into motion, and he lies tense and watchful, certain that he cannot relax and afraid that the next unfamiliar place, the next smell, or the next memory will overtake him again. What finally brought him in was the fear that his shrinking world—work narrowed to what feels safe, conversation softened to avoid disagreement, thoughts forcibly pushed away—was becoming permanent. He hopes to regain some trust in himself and to feel that the future, even at 66, is not already lost.
